meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Sooner or later, we must expand life beyond our little blue mud ball or go extinct'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Elon Musk: from his first-person 2008 Esquire essay on why humanity must become a spacefaring species. Read the original context.

answer.label: Written by

answer.sourceLine: Musk wrote it himself in a first-person essay for Esquire’s “75 Most Influential People of the 21st Century” feature, dated 1 October 2008. The sentence is confirmed word for word in an archived copy of the Esquire page ↗, where a dash comes before “or go extinct.”

source.excerpt: The next big moment will be life becoming multiplanetary, an unprecedented adventure that would dramatically enhance the richness and diversity of our collective consciousness. It would also serve as a hedge against the myriad--and growing--threats to our survival. An asteroid or a supervolcano could certainly destroy us, but we also face risks the dinosaurs never saw: An engineered virus, nuclear war, inadvertent creation of a micro black hole, or some as-yet-unknown technology could spell the end of us. Sooner or later, we must expand life beyond our little blue mud ball--or go extinct.
trail: 2008: Musk’s first-person essay in Esquire’s “75 Most Influential People of the 21st Century” feature contains the exact sentence (archived page ↗).
2010: A blog post that reproduces Wikipedia’s Musk article gives a reworded version: “beyond this green and blue ball” (tetrahedral.blogspot.com ↗).
2017: A reader asked about a paraphrase that used the words “get off of this mud ball.” Quote Investigator traced it to the 2008 Esquire essay and quoted the original passage (Quote Investigator ↗).
Wikiquote lists the sentence among Musk’s sourced quotes for 2008, dated 1 October 2008 and cited to Esquire (Wikiquote ↗).
source.excerptNote: Copied from the archived Esquire page, which prints the dash as a double hyphen (“--”). The next paragraph begins “What stands in the way? The ridiculously recalcitrant problem of big, reusable, reliable rockets.”

author.bio: Elon Musk is a South African–born entrepreneur. He is the chief executive and largest shareholder of Tesla and SpaceX. Esquire’s 2008 profile described him as a PayPal cofounder who was then running Tesla Motors and SolarCity and had founded SpaceX. His stated reason for SpaceX, in this same essay, was to make humanity multiplanetary by cutting the cost of human spaceflight a hundredfold.

misattribution.heading: Reworded versions in circulation
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Musk is correct, but the sentence does not always travel in his exact words.

items.who: “…beyond this green and blue ball — or go extinct”
items.why: This form appears in a May 2010 blog post that reproduces the text of Wikipedia’s Musk article. The Esquire original says “our little blue mud ball” (blog post ↗).
Quote Investigator’s inquiry began with a reader’s loose paraphrase that used these words. QI traced it to Musk’s actual 2008 Esquire sentence (Quote Investigator ↗).
The popular form leaves out the dash before “or go extinct.” The archived Esquire page prints “mud ball--or go extinct” (archived page ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The genuine wording is Musk’s own: “Sooner or later, we must expand life beyond our little blue mud ball—or go extinct,” from his Esquire essay dated 1 October 2008 (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why he wrote it
lead: Musk wrote the essay for Esquire’s 2008 “75 Most Influential People of the 21st Century” feature. It opens by calling the news of the day (the Iraq war, the presidential election and the debt crisis) little more than a footnote. Then it lists the few “genuinely important events” in the history of life on Earth and names life becoming multiplanetary as the next one.

The “blue mud ball” sentence ends his list of threats: asteroids, supervolcanoes, engineered viruses, nuclear war and unknown technologies. It leads into his main point. The obstacle is “big, reusable, reliable rockets,” and the cost of human spaceflight must fall “by a factor of 100.” He then writes, “That’s why I started SpaceX.”
detailsBody: In the same essay Musk writes that recovering and reflying the Falcon 9 would make it “the first fully reusable orbital rocket.” He adds that if launch prices fell enough, “life will become sustainably multiplanetary in less than a century.”
